To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the elimination rate of methylmercury by fish is temperature-dependent, that it decreases with increasing body mass, and that the elimination rate is faster in short-term experiments than in chronic exposure experiments.
Mercury elimination is faster than previously estimated.

the elimination rate of inorganic mercury was 3-fold faster that that of methylmercury and that methylmercury depuration was independent of body size, water temperature, and mercury burden or concentration, and was a first-order process that tended to be over-estimated by a factor of 2.5 by short-term experiments.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elimination of mercury from the bodies of fish.
developing a model of mercury elimination by fish that will be useful for predicting mercury levels in fish in the environment.
the fate and transport of mercury (Hg) in aquatic environments.

the model developed in this study is the first model of its kind to predict methylmercury elimination from fish and that the results of this study will provide a useful framework for the development of a more complex model that will predict mercury elimination in fish.
the model is useful for estimating the elimination rate of Hg from fish, but it should be used with caution and only when data from short-term experiments (< 90 days) are not available.
